newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Taiwan to withdraw SA ambassador, suspend projects.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to withdraw SA ambassador, suspend projects.

text.p: Taiwan Foreign Minister John Chang said on Thursday his country would withdraw its South African ambassador and immediately suspend projects in protest at Pretoria's decision to switch diplomatic ties from Taiwan to China.

Chang told state radio after a meeting with South African Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo that he had been hoping to persuade South Africa to reconsider its decision to end diplomatic links with Taipei in 1997.

Chang, who was reported to be visibly angry, also said the bulk of the 36 existing treaties and agreements between the two countries would be suspended. He added he would meet Taiwanese businessmen on Friday to discuss the issue further.

Taiwan is South Africa's seventh-largest trading partner with two-way trade totalling 5.7 billion rand ($1.24 billion) in 1995. At least 43,000 jobs are expected to be lost if Taiwan disinvests entirely from South Africa.

One investment seen almost sure to be jeopardised by the diplomatic shift is a $3.5 billion petrochemicals plant, which was suggested by Taiwanese vice-premier Hsu Li-teh during an official visit to South Africa in August.
President Nelson Mandela said after a meeting with Chang on Wednesday he would stick by his "agonising" decision to end diplomatic relations with Taiwan but promised to maintain ties in all but name.
He said he was encouraged by remarks by business leaders in Taipei that the end of formal relations would not affect major Taiwanese investments in South Africa.
South Africa was Taiwan's biggest diplomatic ally, its defection to Beijing leaves Taipei with diplomatic relations with just 29 nations, most of them small and poor, which receive Taiwanese aid.
Communists took power in mainland China in 1949 after a civil war that left the former Nationalist government in control only of the island of Taiwan.

Beijing insists Taiwan must come under its control and has waged a successful diplomatic war to isolate Taipei, which lost China's seat at the United Nations in the early 1970s when Washington also switched recognition to Beijing.
South Africa's relations with Taiwan date back to the apartheid era when both were diplomatic pariahs.
